title: Spatiotemporal brain dynamics of limb ownership perception - Nature Communications
byline: Hauser; Maximilian F A; Coppi; Sara; Lundqvist; Daniel; Ehrsson; H Henrik
html:
Abstract

We experience our limbs as our own, but how does the brain generate this fundamental sense of body ownership? Previous studies have relied mainly on fMRI or lesion mapping, providing a static view of the neural mechanisms underlying body ownership. Using magnetoencephalography, robotically controlled visuotactile stimulation, and multivariate analysis across the rubber hand illusion, a real hand condition, and multiple control conditions, we identified source vector dissimilarity patterns reflecting ownership of the left arm. Three phases of ownership-specific activity patterns emerged: (i) anticipatory patterns in medial frontal cortex, right posterior parietal cortex, and right posterior cerebellum before tactile stimulation; (ii) multisensory integration patterns in right dorsal and ventral premotor cortex, right posterior parietal cortex, and anterior cerebellum at 116–156 ms poststimulus; and (iii) later bilateral insular and left hemisphere patterns at 184–232 ms. These findings provide a whole-brain, time-resolved map of activity patterns underlying body ownership, revealing its dynamic neural construction.

Introduction

In most everyday situations, we take the experience that our limbs belong to us for granted, without conscious reflection. When we see our hands, we simply feel that they are our own and part of the rest of our body. However, how does this self-perception of limbs and other body parts arise? This is the problem of body ownership—how we perceptually experience limbs, other body parts, and even the entire body as our own1,2,3,4. Although visual feedback from the body plays an important role in the sense of body ownership, somatosensory inputs from muscles and joints (i.e., proprioception) and the skin (e.g., touch) make critical contributions5,6,7. Thus, the sense of body ownership is typically described as a multisensory perceptual experience of the limbs and body parts that involves continuous integration of signals from multiple sensory modalities8,9,10,11. The resulting perceptual experience of one’s body is fundamental to human conscious experience, critical for the sense of self, and plays an important role in guiding interactions with objects, events, and other living beings in the external world.

Neurological and neuropsychological studies have shown that stroke lesions affecting the premotor cortex, parietal and insular cortices, subcortical regions, and white matter tracts connecting these areas, particularly in the right hemisphere, can disrupt the sense of body ownership of the limbs12,13,14,15,16,17,18,19,20. Such lesions can lead to conditions such as asomatognosia and somatoparaphrenia, in which individuals no longer experience a limb (typically the left arm) as their own, despite seeing it clearly, feeling applied touches, and having some preserved proprioceptive abilities. These findings suggest that intact frontoparietal and subcortical circuits are crucial for generating the normal sense of body ownership. However, lesion studies primarily localize anatomical substrates with relatively low spatial resolution, as lesions are typically large and involve multiple structures within each individual, and they do not elucidate the underlying neural mechanisms with spatial or temporal precision.

The leading experimental paradigm for investigating the sense of body ownership is the rubber hand illusion (RHI)1,6,21,22,23,24. In this bodily illusion24, synchronous touches applied to a rubber hand in full view and to the participant’s real hand, hidden behind a panel, induce the illusory perception that the rubber hand is their own and that the touches and proprioceptive sensations they experience emanate from the rubber hand. The subjective experience of the illusion is typically quantified using questionnaire ratings or psychophysical tasks and complemented by indirect behavioral or psychophysiological measures that reflect changes in multisensory hand representation, such as shifts in perceived hand location toward the rubber hand (proprioceptive drift)22,25,26,27. The illusion depends on principles of multisensory spatial and temporal congruence1,2,4; the more simultaneous and spatially aligned the visual and tactile signals are, the stronger the body ownership illusion becomes28,29,30,31,32. Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) has revealed replicable activation in the premotor cortex, posterior parietal cortex, lateral occipital cortex (LOC), and cerebellum1,33,34,35,36,37. Since the premotor‒parietal areas are associated with the multisensory integration of body-related signals38,39,40,41,42 and their activity correlates with the degree of multisensory spatiotemporal congruence34,43, the strength of the ownership illusion1,35,44, and trial-by-trial detection of the subjective ownership feeling in the RHI34, it has been argued that multisensory integration within these interconnected regions underpins the sense of body ownership1,2,8. However, due to the relatively low temporal resolution of fMRI, which tracks hemodynamic signals that average neural activity over seconds, we currently have a “static” view of brain activity related to body ownership. Thus, we know little about the spatiotemporal dynamics of body ownership activity, that is, how active brain areas interact over time and the relative timing of neural activity in different areas. This knowledge gap is a significant limitation, as such information is crucial for understanding mechanisms that support time-sensitive processes, such as multisensory integration, anticipatory versus bottom-up sensory signals, and the flexible coordination of active networks.

Electroencephalography (EEG) has excellent temporal resolution, but its limited spatial resolution makes comparisons with fMRI literature challenging. For example, Rao and Kayser45 using a RHI paradigm with congruent (illusion) versus incongruent rubber hand orientation (control) under synchronous visuotactile stimulation, reported an attenuation of somatosensory event-related potentials (ERPs) at ~120 ms and 330 ms over frontocentral electrodes, along with decreases in alpha and beta power over frontoparietal regions. Similarly, Sciortino and Kayser46 observed ERP patterns related to the RHI in the time window of ~100–300 ms poststimulus using multivariate classification analyses, revealing distributed frontoparietal patterns. However, the limited spatial resolution of EEG, together with the differences in stimulus protocols, experimental designs, control conditions, and analytical approaches across EEG studies45,46,47,48,49, means that these studies do not provide a detailed picture of the spatiotemporal dynamics of body ownership and that integration with the fMRI literature is lacking. Previous MEG studies have examined somatosensory evoked responses during embodiment manipulations, primarily focusing on modulations in the primary somatosensory cortex50,51. However, these studies did not provide a whole-brain, time-resolved characterization of activity patterns related to body ownership across distributed cortical networks.

In this study, we employed magnetoencephalography (MEG), robotically controlled natural touch stimuli within a classic RHI paradigm, and a comprehensive set of control conditions to characterize the spatiotemporal dynamics of brain activity associated with visuotactile integration in body ownership. Compared with EEG, MEG offers less distorted and more accurate source localization while maintaining millisecond temporal resolution, enabling time-resolved whole-brain activity estimates52. To identify activity patterns associated with body ownership, we used seven conditions, including a left RHI condition, a left real-hand stimulation condition, and appropriate multisensory and unisensory control conditions. We conducted a multivariate GLM-based representational similarity analysis on the whole-brain data to isolate source vector dissimilarity patterns specifically related to visuotactile processes in the context of body ownership from those related to unisensory and nonspecific multisensory effects; this analysis was repeated across successive time points to generate time-resolved maps of body ownership-related activity patterns. Importantly, by identifying such body ownership-specific activity patterns that are shared across both the RHI and a real hand condition, we further isolate patterns that reflect core multisensory processes related to limb ownership and rule out nonspecific illusion-related effects (e.g., surprise or intersensory conflict). Moreover, unlike the vast majority of fMRI studies, which have targeted the right arm, we focused on the left arm because of its greater clinical relevance in the neurological literature on disturbed limb ownership (see the discussion above).

Given this background, we addressed the following key unresolved questions: (1) What are the temporal dynamics of brain activity underlying limb ownership? (2) Which of the occipital, parietal, frontal, insular, and cerebellar regions previously implicated in the fMRI literature exhibit body ownership-related activity patterns within the 100–200 ms poststimulus window, which is known to be critical for the multisensory integration of visual and somatosensory inputs in the association cortex 43,53,54,55? We tested the hypothesis that the premotor cortex, posterior parietal cortex, and cerebellum would show body ownership-related activity reflecting multisensory integration during this window42,45,46,53,56. (3) Can such multisensory integration-related activity patterns be distinguished from those that occur within a prestimulus window, reflecting anticipatory processing54,57,58? We hypothesized that frontal and posterior parietal areas would display body ownership-specific anticipatory activity, as multisensory neurons in these regions signal expected touch before contact54,57,59, and behavioral experiments demonstrate that visually driven predictions contribute to body ownership58,60,61. (4) How do the spatiotemporal dynamics of activity unfold between the two hemispheres during the experience of ownership over the left arm? Based on neuropsychological evidence of right-hemisphere dominance12,13,14,15,16,17,18,19,20 and fMRI findings of bilateral frontoparietal activation in previous RHI studies1,8,33,35,37,62, we predicted predominant right-hemisphere involvement during the critical anticipatory and integration phases. Our MEG results address these questions and reveal time-resolved, whole-brain neural dynamics of body ownership, transforming static network descriptions into a dynamic framework showing how anticipatory processes, multisensory integration, and interhemispheric coordination unfold in time to construct the bodily self.

Results

Forty-five healthy participants underwent magnetoencephalography (MEG) to measure the magnetic fields produced by neural activity in the brain (see Methods and Fig. 1). To induce the RHI, we used an MEG-compatible robotic system to deliver synchronous visual stimulation to a realistic cosmetic left prosthetic hand (the “rubber hand”) in full view and tactile stimulation to the participants’ occluded real left hand. Two robotic arms equipped with brushes delivered brief, controlled taps, with precise temporal control essential for accurate MEG analysis (Fig. 1). Physical brushes ensured natural touch stimulation consistent with the classic RHI setup.

Left panel: Image of a participant seated in the MEG scanner during the RHI. Two pneumatically controlled robotic arms equipped with brushes delivered brief, controlled taps to the index fingers of the visible rubber hand (right side of the occluding screen) and to the participant’s real left hand (out of view, left side of the screen). Right panel: The seven experimental conditions. R denotes the real hand, and F denotes the fake hand. Stimulation sites are indicated in red. For details, see Methods and Table 2.

The experiment included seven different experimental conditions (see Fig. 1 and Methods). In the synchronous congruent (SC) condition, synchronous touches were applied to the real left hand (tactile stimulus) and the rubber hand (visual stimulus), which was placed in a spatially congruent position, mimicking the orientation of a real hand. This condition elicited the RHI, as the multisensory stimulation obeyed the temporal and spatial rules of the RHI1,2,29,30. In the synchronous incongruent (SiC) condition, simultaneous touches were applied, but the rubber hand was rotated 90° counterclockwise relative to the real hand, violating the spatial rule and preventing the RHI6,29. Another control condition (asynchronous congruent, AC) involved asynchronous visual and tactile stimuli delivered to the rubber hand in the congruent position, breaking the illusion by violating the temporal congruence rule30,32. We also included a control condition in which the rubber hand was spatially incongruent (as in the SiC condition) and the stimuli were asynchronous (asynchronous incongruent, AiC). (For the purposes of the MEG analysis, the two asynchronous conditions were each divided into two different event types based on whether the onset time was defined by the tactile or visual stimulus: ACV/ACT and AiCV/AiCT, respectively; see Methods). Additionally, we controlled for and modeled unisensory visual and tactile stimulation effects by including two unisensory conditions: one in which touches were applied only to the congruently placed rubber hand (visual, V) and one in which touches were applied only to the hidden real hand (tactile, T) while the rubber hand was in view. Finally, we included a real hand condition (real, R), in which touches were delivered only to the visible real left hand, with both the rubber hand and the screen removed. This condition allowed us to identify neural activity patterns that are shared across illusory ownership of the rubber hand and the natural sense of ownership of one’s real arm, ensuring that our findings are not driven by processes that arise specifically from the unusual or sensory-conflict-related aspects of the illusion paradigm (e.g., surprise, partially unresolved visuoproprioceptive conflict, or enhanced prediction-error signaling associated with illusion induction). During each condition, participants received repeated brush-tap stimuli at regular intervals (approximately one every 1.5–2 s) over several minutes. Each condition was measured in two separate runs, yielding on the order of 100 trials per run and enabling event-related, time-resolved analysis of neural activity.

Behavioral results

We first analyzed the behavioral data from the entire sample of 45 participants to validate the successful replication of the RHI in the current setup in the MEG scanner. As expected, the questionnaire scores for statement S1 (body ownership; feeling that the rubber hand was one’s own hand) were significantly higher in the SC condition than in the SiC condition (t(44) = 5.17, p < 0.001, pHolm < 0.001, 95% CI [1, 2.29], dz = 0.77, 1-β = 1) (Fig. 2a). Similarly, participants also scored significantly higher for statement S2 (referral of touch; feeling that the touch originated from the rubber hand) in the SC condition than in the SiC condition (V = 508, p = 0.005, pHolm = 0.016, 95% CI [0.5, 2], rC = 0.53, 1-β = 0.97; Fig. 2B). For the control statements (S3–S4), median ratings were negative in both conditions, confirming the rejection of control experiences. Although a small but statistically significant difference between the SC and SiC conditions was observed for S3 (p = 0.032; Fig. 2C), it did not survive Holm correction (pHolm = 0.063). The S4 difference was also not significant (p = 0.275; Fig. 2D). The average illusion strength, which was computed as the mean of S1 and S2 scores, showed a significantly greater difference between SC and SiC than the corresponding difference for the control statements S3 and S4 (t(44) = 2.74, p = 0.009, 95% CI [0.24, 1.56], dz = 0.41, 1-β = 0.76; Fig. 2E), further supporting the specificity of the questionnaire results. As expected, a significant difference in proprioceptive drift was observed between the SC and SiC conditions (t(43) = 3.11, p = 0.003, 95% CI [0.48, 2.24], dz = 0.47, 1-β = 0.86), with SC associated with a greater drift toward the rubber hand (Fig. 2F). Thus, both the questionnaire data and the proprioceptive drift data confirmed the successful induction of the RHI in the current MEG setup. The 30 participants who fulfilled the inclusion criterion for the MEG analysis (see Methods) displayed robust illusion-related effects on both questionnaire ratings and proprioceptive drift (see Supplementary Fig. 1).
